title: AR-DUINO
summary: An active browser-based prototype that turns a physical PCB into an interactive, markerless AR inspection surface while keeping board data, camera frames, and computer-vision processing on the device.
problem: PCB inspection often forces attention to jump between a physical board, a board viewer, component references, and an inspection checklist. That context switching makes it harder to inspect a selected component or net directly on the hardware.
purpose: AR-DUINO explores a static, browser-native workflow for recognizing a flat PCB with a phone camera and projecting the current board selection or inspection step back onto the physical board without sending camera frames to a server.
keyFeatures: Interactive PCB viewer with bundled Arduino UNO and MEGA 2560 samples, pan and zoom, layer controls, selection, and connectivity highlighting.
In-browser parsing support for JSON, EAGLE XML/ZIP, and ODB++ ZIP board data; the current demo intentionally remains sample-first.
Four-corner calibration with an optional bounded edge-detection assist and a preview before applying the board reference.
Markerless planar tracking that recovers with AKAZE features and follows nearby motion with pyramidal Lucas–Kanade optical flow.
Inspection sequences that can guide a component or net step, with pass and flag actions and an AR option to isolate the active target.
On-device developer diagnostics for tracking points and live quality information.
role: I designed and implemented the browser-based PCB viewer and AR inspection prototype, including the board-data workflow, calibration experience, on-device tracking pipeline, projected overlay behavior, and inspection-sequence interactions.
technicalHighlights: All vision work runs in a Web Worker using OpenCV WebAssembly; transferable ImageBitmaps and a one-frame-in-flight scheduler keep camera processing from backing up the main thread.
The tracker combines global AKAZE descriptor recovery with fast local pyramidal Lucas–Kanade tracking, then estimates a planar pose through RANSAC homography.
Quality gates validate inliers, feature coverage, reprojection error, quadrilateral geometry, bounds, and temporal continuity before accepting a pose.
Tracking state moves through TRACKED, SUSPECT, RECOVERING, and LOST modes so an untrustworthy or stale overlay is faded or hidden rather than presented as current.
A shared board model and selection state drive both the flat viewer and AR projection, avoiding a separate AR-only representation of components, nets, and inspection steps.
The projective overlay uses WebGL when available and retains a Canvas2D fallback for broader browser compatibility.

challengesAndSolutions.challenge: Markerless tracking must recover from larger movements while also responding smoothly to smaller frame-to-frame motion.
challengesAndSolutions.solution: The implementation uses AKAZE feature matching for global recovery and pyramidal Lucas–Kanade optical flow for nearby motion, with RANSAC homography joining both paths.

challengesAndSolutions.challenge: A plausible-looking overlay can be unsafe if it is based on weak matches, drift, or an old pose.
challengesAndSolutions.solution: Independent geometric, visual, and temporal quality gates feed explicit tracking states that fade or hide the projection when confidence drops.

challengesAndSolutions.challenge: A browser AR workflow needs to remain responsive on mobile hardware without a backend processing camera video.
challengesAndSolutions.solution: The app keeps processing on-device in a worker, bounds image sizes by performance profile, transfers frames efficiently, and permits only one frame in flight.

challengesAndSolutions.challenge: Inspection guidance can become disconnected from the normal board viewer if it introduces a second state model.
challengesAndSolutions.solution: The AR overlay, viewer, and inspection sequence use the same board model and current selection, so actions in one surface are reflected in the others.

resultsImpact: Demonstrates an on-device, static-web approach to AR-assisted PCB inspection with no camera-frame upload or vision backend.
Provides a guided workflow that can project the selected component, net, or active inspection-sequence step directly onto a matching physical sample board.
Establishes an inspectable prototype baseline for validating browser-based planar tracking across intended boards, lighting conditions, cameras, and device classes.
lessonsLearned: A planar homography is useful for a mostly flat PCB but does not overcome parallax, glare, blur, severe occlusion, lens distortion, or near-edge-on views.
Tracking confidence and failure behavior are part of the interaction design: hiding a stale overlay is more trustworthy than preserving a reassuring but incorrect projection.
Synthetic probes and bundled samples are valuable regression tools, but real-device validation with the target board and operating environment remains essential.
A static browser deployment can keep the complete viewing, parsing, camera, tracking, and overlay workflow local while still requiring HTTPS and feature-aware fallbacks.
